articles.title: That Long Afternoon Nap May Be Quietly Stressing a Diabetic's Liver, a New Study Warns
articles.excerpt: Researchers tracking people with type 2 diabetes found that daytime naps longer than 30 minutes were linked to a higher risk of fatty liver disease — and combined with poor night sleep, the risk more than tripled.
articles.image_caption: A study of people with type 2 diabetes linked daytime naps over 30 minutes to higher fatty-liver risk
articles.nri_angle: The afternoon nap is woven into Indian family life — the post-lunch 'aaram' is practically a cultural institution — even as type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease run rampant through the community. A study suggesting that long naps may be quietly raising liver-disease risk in diabetics speaks directly to a habit most NRI households never think twice about.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Hours of Lifting a Week Cut Women's Heart-Attack Risk by 44 Percent, a Harvard Study of 117,000 Women Finds
articles.excerpt: A new analysis in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology followed women for decades and found that resistance training delivered outsized protection against heart disease — a finding with particular weight for South Asian women, who face heart trouble earlier and harder.
articles.image_caption: A Harvard study of 117,000 women found two hours of resistance training a week cut heart-attack risk by 44%
articles.nri_angle: South Asian women carry an elevated, often under-recognised risk of heart disease, yet strength training remains culturally coded as a man's pursuit in many Indian families. A landmark study showing that just two hours of lifting a week slashes women's heart-attack risk speaks directly to a community where the gym is rarely seen as a place for mothers and aunties — and where the cost of that gap is measured in early heart disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ozempic's Active Ingredient May Quietly Be Protecting Bones, a Study of 60,000 Diabetics Finds
articles.excerpt: Stanford researchers comparing semaglutide against other weight-loss drugs in people with type 2 diabetes found a 15 percent lower fracture risk — a reassuring twist for a community where diabetes is rampant and bones are already thinner.
articles.image_caption: A semaglutide injection pen; a study of 60,000 diabetics linked the drug to 15% fewer fractures
articles.nri_angle: Indians are among the most diabetes-prone people on earth and tend to have lower bone density than Western populations, so a finding that a wildly popular weight-loss drug many NRIs are already taking may also guard against fractures speaks directly to two health risks the diaspora carries at once.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Non-Hormone Pill for Menopause Just Passed Its First Real-World Test — on Hot Flashes and Mood Alike
articles.excerpt: In a study of 656 women, the FDA-approved drug fezolinetant eased hot flashes, night sweats, anxiety and depression within weeks — an option that matters for the many South Asian women who avoid or cannot take hormone therapy.
articles.image_caption: A study of 656 women found the non-hormone drug fezolinetant eased hot flashes and mood within weeks
articles.nri_angle: Menopause remains a taboo, under-treated subject in many Indian families, and cultural wariness about hormone therapy leaves countless diaspora women suffering in silence — so evidence that a non-hormonal pill measurably eases hot flashes, sleep loss and mood is exactly the kind of option that could reach women who would never consider hormones.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Smartwatch on Your Wrist May Be Quietly Doing Your Heart a Favour, a Review of 14 Trials Finds
articles.excerpt: Pooling 14 clinical trials, researchers found that heart-disease patients who used fitness apps or wearables walked nearly 1,100 more steps a day than those who did not — a small, low-cost nudge with outsized relevance for a community that develops heart disease early.
articles.image_caption: A fitness tracker; a review of 14 trials found heart patients using such tools walked about 1,100 more steps daily
articles.nri_angle: People of Indian origin suffer heart attacks up to a decade earlier than other populations and are among the most enthusiastic adopters of smartwatches and fitness rings — so the finding that a device many NRIs already wear can measurably push them to move more turns a gadget on the wrist into a genuine, low-cost cardiac-prevention tool for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Head Injury Can Raise the Risk of Brain Disease. New Research Says the Danger May Run Both Ways.
articles.excerpt: A study of more than 55,000 older veterans finds that those recently diagnosed with stroke, dementia, epilepsy or Parkinson's were far more likely to have suffered a traumatic brain injury — a finding that reframes fall prevention as brain protection for ageing parents.
articles.image_caption: An older adult walking with support; falls are the main cause of traumatic brain injury in the elderly
articles.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs are caring for ageing parents — some living abroad with them, many supporting elders back in India from a distance — and this research delivers a sharp, actionable warning: a parent newly diagnosed with dementia, stroke, epilepsy or Parkinson's is in a high-risk window for a fall-related head injury, making home fall-proofing one of the most concrete things a diaspora family can do.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Carrying Extra Weight Now Linked to 19 Cancers, Not 13 — and South Asians Show Up in the Fine Print
articles.excerpt: Pooling more than 1.5 million cancer cases across 23 countries, a sweeping new review widens the list of weight-related cancers and finds the risks differ sharply by sex and region — with striking gaps in data on South Asian populations.
articles.image_caption: A waist measurement; a review of 1.5 million cancer cases links higher BMI to 19 cancer types
articles.nri_angle: South Asians develop diabetes and heart disease at lower body weights than Western populations, yet this very review flags that South Asia is badly under-represented in long-term cancer data — meaning diaspora families are being handed risk numbers built largely on European and East Asian bodies, and should treat even a modest waistline as a cancer-prevention issue, not just a cosmetic one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Weight-Loss Drugs May Do Something Unexpected for Men: Lift Testosterone and Improve Sperm
articles.excerpt: Early data presented at a major endocrinology meeting suggests GLP-1 medicines like Ozempic may raise testosterone and improve sperm quality in men with obesity — a tentative finding in a field where male fertility is rarely discussed openly.
articles.image_caption: A GLP-1 injection pen; early data suggests the weight-loss drugs may improve testosterone and sperm quality in men
articles.nri_angle: Male infertility is one of the most stigmatised and silently borne health issues in Indian families, where the burden of childlessness is too often placed on women; framing it as a treatable, hormonally-influenced medical condition — one that weight and metabolic health can move — gives diaspora couples a less shame-laden, more clinical way to seek help.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Harvard Just Found the Strength-Training Sweet Spot for a Longer Life. It Is Less Than You Think.
articles.excerpt: Following 150,000 adults for more than three decades, researchers report that about 90 to 120 minutes of strength training a week is tied to the biggest drop in the risk of early death — and that piling on far more brings little extra benefit.
articles.image_caption: Strength training with weights; a 30-year study of 150,000 adults found 90-120 minutes a week is the longevity sweet spot
articles.nri_angle: Strength training is the great blind spot in many Indian-origin households — elders walk for cardio but rarely lift, even as South Asians carry more body fat and less muscle for their size, raising diabetes and heart risk; a finding that just 15-20 minutes of resistance work a day moves the longevity needle makes the habit feel achievable rather than gym-bro intimidating.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Pill May Be Quietly Driving Food Cravings, a Study of Young Women Finds
articles.excerpt: Tracking 422 women over two menstrual cycles, researchers found binge-eating episodes rose on the days they took active birth control pills — a hormonal link that held even after accounting for mood and other medications.
articles.image_caption: Combined oral contraceptive pills; a study links active-pill days to more binge-eating episodes in young women
articles.nri_angle: Disordered eating is heavily stigmatised and rarely discussed in Indian families, and the contraceptive pill is increasingly used by young diaspora women — so framing sudden food cravings as a possible hormonal side effect, not a failure of willpower, gives mothers and daughters a less shame-laden way to talk about both binge eating and birth control.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Weight-Loss Drugs Were Supposed to Get People Moving. A New Study Found They Quietly Sit Down More.
articles.excerpt: Tracking 753 adults on Ozempic-style medications with fitness monitors, researchers found their daily steps and exercise minutes fell after starting the drugs — not rose. Because these medications strip away muscle along with fat, the slump is exactly the wrong response, and it carries a sharp warning for the growing number of diaspora families now reaching for them.
articles.image_caption: An injection pen; a study of 753 GLP-1 users found their daily steps and exercise fell after starting the drugs
articles.nri_angle: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy are spreading fast through Indian-American and broader diaspora households already at elevated risk of muscle-poor, fat-heavy bodies and early diabetes; this study warns that the very people most drawn to the injections may be undercutting them by moving less, and losing the muscle they can least afford to lose.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Cheapest Protein in the Indian Kitchen May Be the Most Protective. New Research Keeps Pointing to the Humble Dal.
articles.excerpt: A run of nutrition research keeps landing on the same unglamorous conclusion: legumes — the lentils, chickpeas and beans at the heart of Indian cooking — lower blood pressure, protect the heart and, in one landmark study of older adults, were the single most protective food group for survival. For a diaspora drifting toward Western convenience food, it is a reminder that the answer was on the thali all along.
articles.image_caption: Lentils and legumes; research repeatedly links the cheap pantry staple to lower blood pressure and longer survival
articles.nri_angle: Lentils, chickpeas and beans are the protein backbone of Indian vegetarian cooking, yet many diaspora families quietly eat less dal as schedules tighten and Western convenience food creeps in; the science says the cheapest item in their pantry is also one of the most protective against the heart disease and diabetes that strike South Asians early.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Study of 5,700 Teenagers Found What Wrecks Their Sleep — and Girls Are Paying the Steeper Price
articles.excerpt: In a survey of 5,713 adolescents published in PLOS One, a third had poor sleep quality, and the biggest culprits were a familiar trio: mental health, body weight and screen time. Girls fared markedly worse than boys. For diaspora parents fighting the nightly battle over phones, the findings put hard numbers on an instinct they already had.
articles.image_caption: A teenager on a phone at night; a study of 5,713 adolescents tied poor sleep to screen time, body weight and mental health
articles.nri_angle: Diaspora parents wage a near-universal nightly struggle over screens and sleep with teenagers caught between academic pressure and phones; this large study names the three levers — screen time, weight and mental health — that actually move adolescent sleep, and flags that daughters may be carrying a heavier burden.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A High-Dose Omega-3 Pill Was Supposed to Sharpen Aging Brains. A Two-Year Trial Found It Did Nothing.
articles.excerpt: In a rigorous randomized trial published this week in the Lancet journal eBioMedicine, two years of high-dose DHA supplements raised omega-3 levels in the blood and even the brain — yet produced no improvement in memory, cognition or the size of the brain's memory centre. For a diaspora that treats fish-oil capsules as a daily insurance policy, the finding is a pointed reality check.
articles.image_caption: Omega-3 fish-oil capsules; a two-year randomized trial found high-dose DHA failed to improve memory or cognition in at-risk older adults
articles.nri_angle: Fish-oil and omega-3 capsules are among the most popular supplements in Indian-American medicine cabinets, often taken specifically to protect aging memory; this gold-standard trial suggests that for people who are otherwise unhealthy, the pills do not deliver the brain benefit so many quietly count on.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Common Vitamin B3 Supplement Helped Older Adults With Clogged Leg Arteries Walk Farther, a New Trial Finds
articles.excerpt: In a six-month double-blind trial from Northwestern and the University of Florida, older adults with peripheral artery disease who took nicotinamide riboside — a form of vitamin B3 that boosts the cellular fuel NAD — walked meaningfully farther than those on a placebo, with the biggest gains among those who took their pills faithfully. Adding red-wine compound resveratrol added nothing.
articles.image_caption: Older adults walking; a vitamin B3 supplement that boosts cellular NAD modestly improved walking distance in people with peripheral artery disease
articles.nri_angle: Peripheral artery disease tracks closely with the diabetes and heart disease that strike South Asians early and hard, and supervised walking therapy is often out of reach for elders living far from medical centres or with family; an affordable daily supplement that modestly improves mobility speaks directly to that gap.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Cheap Diabetes Drug Was Hailed as a Longevity Pill. A 21-Year Study Says Diet and Exercise Beat It.
articles.excerpt: Tracking adults with prediabetes for more than two decades, researchers found that an intensive diet-and-exercise program lowered the risk of piling up multiple chronic diseases — while metformin, the drug touted as an anti-ageing wonder, did no better than a placebo.
articles.image_caption: A diet rich in vegetables and regular exercise; a 21-year study found lifestyle change, not metformin, cut the risk of multiple chronic diseases
articles.nri_angle: South Asians develop prediabetes and Type 2 diabetes earlier and at lower body weights than almost any other group, and metformin is one of the most prescribed drugs in Indian households worldwide — so the finding that a structured diet-and-exercise routine, not the pill, is what actually held off the cascade of chronic disease over 21 years speaks directly to how the NRI community should weight medication against daily habits.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Vitamin in Your Morning Orange May Help Keep Your Brain Younger, a Study of 2,000 Adults Finds
articles.excerpt: Japanese researchers measured vitamin C directly in the blood of older adults — not just their diets — and found that those with higher levels had better-preserved gray matter and stronger connections in a brain network central to memory.
articles.image_caption: Citrus fruit, a key vitamin C source; a study links higher blood vitamin C to better-preserved brain structure in older adults
articles.nri_angle: Vegetarian and plant-forward Indian diets are often rich in vitamin C from citrus, amla, guava, peppers and leafy greens — but the heavy boiling and long cooking common in desi kitchens destroys much of it, making this a rare case where a traditional diaspora strength can quietly become a deficiency that may matter for the ageing brain.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Eat More Plant Polyphenols and You May Hurt Less — New Research Links Diet to Migraine Relief
articles.excerpt: A study published this month in PLOS One found that people who ate more polyphenol-rich foods — berries, green tea, coffee, herbs and spices — reported lower pain sensitivity and less migraine-related disability. For a diaspora whose traditional kitchen is built on turmeric, ginger and green tea, the implications are quietly encouraging.
articles.image_caption: Green tea, berries and spices are rich in polyphenols; new research links higher polyphenol intake to lower pain sensitivity and migraine disability
articles.nri_angle: Migraine is strikingly common among South Asian women, and the polyphenols this study credits with easing pain — from turmeric and ginger to green tea and spices — are precisely the compounds that fill a traditional Indian kitchen, suggesting the diaspora may already hold a dietary lever it rarely thinks to pull.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Not All Vegetarian Diets Are Equal: A 400,000-Person Study Shows Why the Quality of Plant Foods Decides Your Health
articles.excerpt: Pooling data from more than 407,000 adults across Europe and Britain, researchers found that a diet built on healthy plant foods sharply lowered the risk of developing both cancer and heart-and-metabolic disease together — while a plant-based diet heavy on refined grains, sugar and fried food did the opposite. The effect was strongest in adults under 60.
articles.image_caption: Lentils, vegetables and whole grains; a 400,000-person study shows the quality of plant foods, not the vegetarian label, decides health outcomes
articles.nri_angle: The Indian diaspora often equates 'vegetarian' with 'healthy' — yet a diet of white rice, fried snacks, sweets and refined flour is plant-based and harmful, while one of dal, vegetables and whole grains is plant-based and protective; this study draws exactly that line, and it matters enormously for a community already prone to diabetes and heart disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Bad Sleep in Your Forties and Fifties May Quietly Shape How You Feel a Decade Later — Especially for Women
articles.excerpt: A study presented at SLEEP 2026 tracked nearly 600 middle-aged and older adults for nine years and found that those who struggled to sleep ended up with lower psychological well-being years on. The link held firm for women but faded for men once other factors were stripped out.
articles.image_caption: A person lying awake at night; a new study links midlife sleep problems to lower well-being a decade later, especially in women
articles.nri_angle: Sleep is the first thing to go for diaspora women juggling demanding careers, young children and ageing parents across time zones — and this research suggests the broken nights of midlife are not just an inconvenience but a long-term risk to how they will feel and function a decade from now.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cutting Out Sugar Entirely Sounds Healthy. A New Study Suggests It Can Backfire on Your Gut.
articles.excerpt: Researchers at Kuwait's Dasman Diabetes Institute fed mice a low-fat diet for 16 weeks — one group with table sugar, one with none at all. The completely sugar-free group did not gain weight, but developed disrupted gut bacteria, inflammation, insulin resistance and early signs of fatty liver.
articles.image_caption: White sugar; a new study suggests cutting sucrose out entirely can disrupt gut health and metabolism
articles.nri_angle: Diaspora families are increasingly going 'sugar-free' to fight the community's high rates of diabetes — swapping out everything from chai sugar to sweets — yet this research is an early warning that the goal should be balance and moderation, not total elimination, especially for a population already prone to metabolic disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Scientists Found the Muscle Switch That Exercise Flips On. It May Explain Why Movement Keeps You Strong With Age.
articles.excerpt: A protein called NOX4 falls as we grow older and inactive — and when researchers stripped it from muscle, animals grew frail, lost muscle and developed insulin resistance. Exercise restored it, offering a molecular clue to why staying active protects the ageing body.
articles.image_caption: Strength training in older age; new research links the muscle protein NOX4 to how exercise preserves strength
articles.nri_angle: South Asians lose muscle earlier and carry more body fat at the same weight than most populations, making age-related frailty and insulin resistance a quiet diaspora epidemic — and this research underlines that for the NRI parent or professional, regular movement is not optional but a biological necessity that flips on the body's own repair machinery.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It Is Not Just How High Your Blood Pressure Is. How Much It Swings May Quietly Age Your Brain.
articles.excerpt: A Monash University study tracking blood pressure around the clock found that bigger 24-hour swings were tied to worse memory and problem-solving — a decline equivalent to roughly seven extra years of brain ageing — and to visible signs of injury on brain scans.
articles.image_caption: A blood pressure measurement; a new study links 24-hour swings in blood pressure to poorer brain health
articles.nri_angle: Hypertension is rampant and frequently undertreated among South Asians, and most diaspora families judge it by a single clinic reading — yet this research suggests the hidden danger lies in the swings between readings, a pattern only round-the-clock monitoring can catch, reframing how NRIs should manage their own and their ageing parents' blood pressure.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It May Not Be Just What's in Ultra-Processed Foods That Hurts You — It's How They're Made
articles.excerpt: A new Tufts University analysis of two decades of US health data found that people who ate more ultra-processed foods had worse health and a higher risk of early death — even after accounting for the nutrition inside the food. The processing itself, the researchers argue, may carry an independent harm.
articles.image_caption: Packaged ultra-processed foods; a Tufts analysis found their industrial processing may harm health independent of the nutrition they contain
articles.nri_angle: Indian and South Asian families increasingly lean on packaged namkeen, instant mixes, sugary biscuits and ready meals as life gets busier abroad — and this research suggests the industrial processing in those products may damage health in ways that reading the nutrition label alone will never reveal.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Most Addictive Foods Aren't Only the Sugary Ones. A New Study Points the Finger at Refined Starch.
articles.excerpt: Researchers analyzing why ultra-processed foods are so hard to stop eating found that the usual villain — sugar — is only half the story. Rapidly digested refined carbohydrates, even in savory snacks with little or no added sugar, may be just as powerful a driver of cravings.
articles.image_caption: Savory snacks like potato chips and fried namkeen deliver rapidly digested refined starch that researchers link to hard-to-stop cravings
articles.nri_angle: South Asian snacking culture is built on refined-flour and rapidly-digested treats — namkeen, sev, mathri, fried maida snacks and white-rice indulgences — and this research suggests these savory staples may hijack appetite as effectively as anything sweet, a blind spot for a community already prone to diabetes.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Cheap Amino-Acid Supplement Plus Exercise Cut Older Adults' Fatigue Almost in Half, a Pilot Trial Finds
articles.excerpt: In a controlled study of obese older adults, those who paired eight weeks of exercise with branched-chain amino acids saw fatigue fall 45 percent and depressive symptoms drop — while the placebo group's tiredness nearly doubled. The findings hint at a low-cost way to help aging bodies recover from the very exercise meant to keep them strong.
articles.image_caption: Older adults exercising; a UT Health San Antonio pilot trial found branched-chain amino acids cut fatigue 45 percent when paired with exercise
articles.nri_angle: Many diaspora families care for aging parents who eat largely vegetarian diets that can fall short on the leucine-rich protein that guards against age-related muscle loss — making an affordable amino-acid strategy especially relevant for South Asian elders at high risk of sarcopenia and frailty.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Bad Sleep May Do More Than Tire You Out — A Study of 1.8 Million People Links Insomnia to an Irregular Heartbeat
articles.excerpt: In one of the largest analyses of its kind, Japanese researchers found that people with insomnia had a 14 percent higher chance of developing atrial fibrillation, the irregular heart rhythm that raises the risk of stroke. The link was strongest in women and in adults under 65.
articles.image_caption: A study of 1.8 million people linked insomnia to a 14 percent higher risk of atrial fibrillation, with the strongest effect in women and adults under 65
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry a well-documented double burden of disrupted sleep and early heart disease, and diaspora life adds its own insomnia triggers — late-night calls across time zones, shift work and chronic stress — making the sleep-heart connection especially worth heeding for the community.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Single Gut Microbe Helped People Keep the Weight Off. A New Trial Puts a Number on It.
articles.excerpt: In a randomized trial published in Nature Medicine, adults who took a daily dose of a pasteurized gut bacterium after dieting regained far less weight than those on a placebo — 2.6 pounds versus 7.1 — over six months. It is the clearest human evidence yet that the bug in your gut may decide whether the kilos stay off.
articles.image_caption: An illustration of gut microbiota; a Nature Medicine trial found a pasteurized gut bacterium cut weight regain by more than half
articles.nri_angle: South Asians are uniquely prone to regaining weight as dangerous visceral fat after dieting, and to the early diabetes that follows — a microbiome-based tool that helps the weight stay off could matter more for the diaspora than for almost any other group.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The People You Live With Are Quietly Rewiring Your Gut. A New Study Maps How Microbes Spread Under One Roof.
articles.excerpt: Researchers found that people who share a home share a quarter of their oral microbes — and romantic partners share far more — regardless of whether they eat the same food. The finding reframes health as something families pass between one another, microbe by microbe.
articles.image_caption: A family sharing a meal; new research finds people who live together share about a quarter of their oral microbes
articles.nri_angle: Multigenerational living — grandparents, parents and children under one roof — is a hallmark of diaspora households, which means the microbes, and the health risks and benefits they carry, are shared more intensely in Indian families than in the nuclear homes this kind of research usually studies.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Longevity Sweet Spot Is Not the Gym Rat's. Just 90 Minutes of Weights a Week Cut Death Risk in a 30-Year Study.
articles.excerpt: Harvard researchers followed nearly 150,000 adults for three decades and found that 90 to 119 minutes of strength training a week was the dose linked to the lowest risk of dying — from any cause, from heart disease and from brain disease. Pile on more and the benefit flattens. Pair it with cardio and it deepens.
articles.image_caption: A person training with dumbbells; a 30-year study found 90 to 119 minutes of weekly strength work cut death risk most
articles.nri_angle: South Asians lose muscle earlier and carry more dangerous visceral fat than most populations, yet weight training is still treated as vanity in many diaspora households — this 30-year study reframes a modest 90 minutes a week of resistance work as a longevity prescription, not gym vanity.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: You Do Not Need to Sit Less. You Need to Stand Up More Often. A New Trial Found Rising From Your Chair Lowers Blood Pressure.
articles.excerpt: A UC San Diego study put post-menopausal women through three months of small changes and found something counterintuitive: simply standing up more frequently — about 25 extra times a day — nudged down blood pressure, while merely sitting less did not deliver a clear win.
articles.image_caption: An older woman rising from a chair; a UCSD trial found standing up more often lowered blood pressure
articles.nri_angle: Diaspora women, especially after menopause, carry an outsized burden of hypertension and heart disease that often goes under-treated — and this study offers a no-cost, no-equipment habit that fits the desk-bound, family-juggling reality of many Indian-American households.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Skinny Jab Has a Hidden Catch. People on Ozempic Are Quietly Moving Less, Not More.
articles.excerpt: A first-of-its-kind study tracking the Fitbit data of more than 750 adults found that daily steps and exercise both fell after they started a GLP-1 weight-loss drug — the opposite of what most assume. Because these medicines also strip away muscle, doctors warn that moving is no longer optional.
articles.image_caption: A semaglutide injection pen; a new study found activity fell after people started GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
articles.nri_angle: GLP-1 jabs are sweeping through diaspora WhatsApp groups and family circles as the fix for the stubborn 'thin-fat' South Asian midriff — but this study warns that losing weight on the drug while moving less can shed the very muscle that protects against the community's early diabetes and heart disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Two-Year Brain Experiment Just Proved You Can Slow Mental Decline. The Recipe Is Boring — and It Works.
articles.excerpt: The landmark US POINTER trial put more than 2,000 at-risk older adults on a structured plan of exercise, the MIND diet, brain training and health check-ins. After two years, the group with the most structure and accountability showed measurably better thinking and memory than those left to do it alone.
articles.image_caption: Older adults exercising together; the US POINTER trial paired structured exercise with diet and brain training
articles.nri_angle: Dementia carries deep stigma and few answers in many Indian families, where ageing parents are cared for at home; this trial offers a low-cost, drug-free playbook — much of it built on movement, vegetables, lentils and community — that maps neatly onto how the diaspora already lives.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Five-a-Day May Not Be Enough for Your Heart. The Foods That Matter Most Are Hiding in Plain Sight.
articles.excerpt: A study of more than 30,000 adults in the US and UK found that even people who hit their fruit-and-vegetable targets rarely got enough flavanols — the plant compounds tied to a sharply lower risk of dying from heart disease. The fix is in specific foods: berries, apples with skin, beans and green tea.
articles.image_caption: Berries and green tea are among the richest sources of heart-protective flavanols
articles.nri_angle: The diaspora dutifully fills the fridge with fruit and vegetables, but a new analysis shows the heart benefit hinges on which ones — and several of the richest sources (apples, beans, the chai-adjacent habit of green tea) slot easily into an Indian kitchen already built around dal, sabzi and a daily cup.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Three Servings of Whole Grains a Day Kept the Waistline in Check for 18 Years. The Refined Stuff Did the Opposite.
articles.excerpt: Tracking more than 3,100 adults for nearly two decades, researchers using data from one of the longest-running heart studies found that people who ate at least three daily servings of whole grains gained far less around the middle — and saw smaller rises in blood sugar and blood pressure — than those who leaned on refined grains.
articles.image_caption: Whole grains; a near-18-year study tied three daily servings to a slower-growing waistline
articles.nri_angle: The diaspora plate runs heavy on white rice and refined-flour rotis, naan and parathas — exactly the foods this 18-year study ties to a creeping waistline and rising blood sugar; swapping in brown rice, whole-wheat atta, millets and oats is a low-effort move against the abdominal fat that drives South Asian diabetes.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
